questions.question: Why are special methods needed in developmental psychobiology?
options: Brain structure cannot be studied until adolescence with non-invasive techniques
Infants and young children may not understand instructions or provide reliable verbal reports
Young participants cannot show measurable physiological responses during development
Behavioral measures are unsuitable for studying perception or attention in infancy during normal developmental testing
questions.feedback: Infants and young children cannot always understand instructions, give verbal reports, or perform complex tasks.

questions.question: Which type of measure uses observable actions as an index of perception, attention, learning, or memory?
options: Peripheral physiological measures
Neural recording methods
Neuroimaging measures
Behavioral methods
questions.feedback: Behavioral methods use observable behavior as an index of internal processes.

questions.question: What becomes the dependent variable when an infant cannot verbally report what they perceive or remember?
options: The participant's age at the time of testing
The infant's measurable behavior
Only the anatomical structure of the brain
The experimenter's interpretation of the stimulus
questions.feedback: In behavioral developmental methods, measurable behavior itself can become the dependent variable.

questions.question: What is the orienting response?
options: A decrease in response after many presentations of the same stimulus
A coordinated response to a novel or salient event that captures attention
A learned head turn reinforced by an interesting visual event
A preference for a familiar stimulus over a novel stimulus
questions.feedback: The orienting response is the coordinated response produced when a novel or salient event captures attention.

questions.question: What is the basic logic of an expectancy-violation experiment?
options: Comparing looking at expected and unexpected events
Rewarding a head turn following a change in sound
Presenting the same stimulus until the response decreases
Measuring electrical potentials from scalp electrodes
questions.feedback: Expectancy-violation paradigms compare responses to expected events with responses to unexpected or impossible events.

questions.question: Why must longer looking at an unexpected event be interpreted carefully?
options: Because infants cannot move their eyes before one year of age
Because unexpected events always produce the same response during the relevant experimental condition
Because perceptual salience can also influence looking time
Because looking time is unrelated to visual processing in infancy
questions.feedback: Perceptual salience can also influence looking, so appropriate controls are necessary.

questions.question: What is habituation?
options: A conditioned movement produced only after reinforcement is removed
A neural response measured by averaging EEG trials across events in the method described in the lecture
A progressive decrease in response after repeated presentation of the same stimulus
A progressive increase in response whenever a familiar stimulus is repeated during normal developmental testing
questions.feedback: Habituation is the progressive reduction of a response when the same stimulus is presented repeatedly.

questions.question: What does recovery of responding to a new stimulus after habituation suggest?
options: The infant has lost sensitivity to the sensory modality
The new stimulus was necessarily more intense than the original one
The infant can no longer remember the habituated stimulus
The infant detected a difference between the old and new stimuli
questions.feedback: Recovery after habituation indicates that the infant detected a difference between the habituated and test stimuli.

questions.question: What is conditioned head turning commonly used to test?
options: Visual acuity in this developmental paradigm
Blood oxygenation
Auditory discrimination
Cortical myelination in this developmental paradigm
questions.feedback: Once learned, conditioned head turning can be used to test auditory discrimination.

questions.question: What does preferential looking measure?
options: How long an infant looks at alternative visual stimuli
How rapidly neural activity changes after a sound
How strongly an infant sucks on a pressure-sensitive pacifier in the method described in the lecture
How much radioactive tracer accumulates in a brain region
questions.feedback: Preferential looking measures differences in looking time between alternative visual stimuli.

questions.question: What do Teller acuity cards estimate?
options: Visual acuity
Heart-rate variability
Recognition memory in the method described in the lecture
Auditory discrimination in this developmental paradigm
questions.feedback: Teller acuity cards use preferential looking to estimate visual acuity.

questions.question: How are Teller acuity cards used?
options: EEG is recorded while the infant views a uniform field during the relevant experimental condition
The infant hears tones of progressively increasing frequency
The infant presses a button whenever a grating appears
Progressively finer gratings are shown until reliable orientation is no longer detected
questions.feedback: Progressively finer gratings are shown until the observer can no longer reliably determine where the infant is looking.

questions.question: What is the Visual Paired Comparison task used to study?
options: Cortical blood flow using near-infrared light
Neural oscillations using scalp electrodes
Motor control through rewarded head turning
Recognition and memory through familiar-versus-novel looking
questions.feedback: Visual Paired Comparison uses familiar-versus-novel looking to study recognition and memory.

questions.question: What is one advantage of peripheral physiological measures in developmental studies?
options: They provide better spatial localization than structural MRI
They can be useful when overt behavior is small, unreliable, or unavailable
They always identify the exact cognitive process involved
They directly measure single-neuron action potentials
questions.feedback: Peripheral physiological measures can be useful when overt behavior is small, unreliable, or unavailable.

questions.question: Why is heart-rate variability described as informative but not specific?
options: Because a change in HRV does not identify the exact cognitive process that caused it
Because it requires ionizing radiation as the principal measurement used here as the main index of the process being studied
Because it can only be measured in adults as the principal measurement used here when the participant is tested in this paradigm
Because it cannot change during attention in the method described in the lecture when the participant is tested in this paradigm
questions.feedback: A change in HRV can accompany attention or arousal without uniquely identifying the cognitive process.

questions.question: What is non-nutritive sucking?
options: A reflex produced only when food is delivered as the main index of the process being studied
Spontaneous sucking on a pacifier or nipple without feeding
A method for measuring cortical electrical potentials as the primary signal recorded in this technique
A behavioral response available only after language develops during the relevant experimental condition
questions.feedback: Non-nutritive sucking is spontaneous sucking on a pacifier or nipple without feeding.

questions.question: What is the core manipulation in the high-amplitude sucking paradigm?
options: A head turn switches off the stimulus
Sucks above a threshold trigger a stimulus
Visual stimuli appear only when the infant looks away
Sounds are presented randomly and independently of behavior
questions.feedback: In high-amplitude sucking, sufficiently strong sucks trigger presentation of a stimulus.

questions.question: What did the Vouloumanos and Werker experiment compare?
options: Speech sounds before and after sleep as the main index of the process being studied
High- and low-spatial-frequency gratings
Speech with non-speech sounds using high-amplitude sucking
Familiar faces with novel faces
questions.feedback: The experiment used high-amplitude sucking to compare newborn responses to speech and non-speech sounds.

questions.question: What response pattern to speech and non-speech is described in the deck?
options: Responses increased only for non-speech and disappeared for speech in the method described in the lecture
Responses habituated equally quickly to both sound categories
Responses habituated to non-speech while remaining higher or showing little habituation to speech
Responses were identical because newborns could not discriminate the sounds during the relevant experimental condition
questions.feedback: The deck reports habituation to non-speech sounds, while responses to speech remained high or showed little habituation.

questions.question: What methodological trade-off is illustrated by EEG and fMRI?
options: Behavioral response versus verbal report
Temporal resolution versus spatial localization
Familiarity versus perceptual preference
Direct versus radioactive measurement
questions.feedback: EEG has excellent temporal resolution but limited spatial localization, whereas fMRI has better localization but slower timing.

questions.question: What does EEG record?
options: Magnetic fields induced by a TMS coil during normal developmental testing
Differences in electrical potential from scalp electrodes
Changes in near-infrared light absorption in this developmental paradigm
Changes in radioactive tracer concentration as the principal measurement used here
questions.feedback: EEG records differences in electrical potential using electrodes placed on the scalp.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of EEG in developmental research?
options: It gives precise anatomical images of deep structures when the participant is tested in this paradigm
It offers millisecond timing and can be used during passive stimulation
It identifies individual action potentials at the scalp
It measures hemodynamics with excellent spatial resolution
questions.feedback: EEG is non-invasive, silent, suitable for passive stimulation, and has millisecond temporal resolution.

questions.question: What does scalp EEG mainly reflect according to the deck?
options: Radioactive decay events in metabolically active brain tissue
Changes in cerebral blood flow produced by metabolic demand during the relevant experimental condition
Summed electrical fields from synchronized postsynaptic currents in cortical populations
Individual action potentials from single neurons beneath each electrode as the primary signal recorded in this technique
questions.feedback: Scalp EEG mainly reflects population-level electrical fields generated by synchronized postsynaptic currents.

questions.question: Which EEG frequency band is approximately 8-13 Hz?
options: Delta in the method described in the lecture
Beta during the relevant experimental condition
Alpha
Gamma during the relevant experimental condition
questions.feedback: The deck defines the alpha band as approximately 8-13 Hz.

questions.question: What does spectral analysis of spontaneous EEG do?
options: It identifies cortical anatomy with magnetic resonance during normal developmental testing
It measures gamma-photon arrival times in this developmental paradigm
It decomposes the signal into its frequency content
It averages repeated events to isolate an ERP as the principal measurement used here
questions.feedback: Spectral analysis decomposes EEG into frequency components and quantifies activity across bands.

questions.question: How is an event-related potential obtained?
options: By measuring spontaneous EEG without event timing during the relevant experimental condition
By injecting a tracer and reconstructing metabolism
By applying a magnetic pulse and measuring behavior in this developmental paradigm
By aligning EEG to repeated events and averaging across trials
questions.feedback: ERPs are obtained by aligning EEG activity to repeated events and averaging across trials.

questions.question: Why does averaging help reveal an ERP?
options: It reduces activity that is not consistently time-locked to the event
It removes every low-frequency component
It increases activity unrelated to event timing in the method described in the lecture
It converts electrical activity into a hemodynamic response as the principal measurement used here
questions.feedback: Averaging reduces activity that is not consistently time-locked and emphasizes reproducible event-related activity.

questions.question: What does MEG measure?
options: Gamma photons from positron annihilation as the primary signal recorded in this technique
Scalp electrical potentials
Tiny magnetic fields generated by neuronal electrical currents
Changes in blood oxygenation
questions.feedback: MEG measures tiny magnetic fields generated by neuronal electrical currents.

questions.question: What makes fetal MEG useful for developmental research?
options: It produces structural images of fetal white matter
It uses ionizing radiation to measure metabolism before birth as the primary signal recorded in this technique
It can non-invasively detect fetal brain activity through the maternal abdomen
It directly measures fetal neurotransmitter concentrations
questions.feedback: Fetal MEG can detect magnetic fields generated by the fetal brain through the maternal abdomen.

questions.question: Which methods are presented as direct measures of electromagnetic consequences of neural activity?
options: PET and fMRI in this developmental paradigm
TMS and structural MRI
fMRI and fNIRS as the primary signal recorded in this technique
EEG and MEG
questions.feedback: EEG and MEG measure electrical or magnetic signals generated directly by neural activity.

questions.question: Which methods are presented as indirect measures of physiological consequences of neural activity?
options: fMRI, fNIRS, and PET
TMS and EEG only as the main index of the process being studied
EEG and MEG only as the principal measurement used here
Conditioned head turning and EEG
questions.feedback: fMRI, fNIRS, and PET measure physiological consequences such as oxygenation, blood flow, or metabolism.

questions.question: What is neurovascular coupling?
options: A mechanism converting scalp potentials into magnetic fields as the primary signal recorded in this technique
The link between local neural activity and changes in blood flow, volume, and oxygenation
A method for reconstructing gamma-photon events
A reduction in response after repeated stimuli in this developmental paradigm in the method described in the lecture
questions.feedback: Neurovascular coupling links local neural activity to changes in blood flow, blood volume, and hemoglobin oxygenation.

questions.question: What does diffusion MRI or DTI investigate in the deck?
options: Peripheral autonomic arousal
Organization of white-matter pathways
Auditory mismatch responses in this developmental paradigm
Postsynaptic receptor clustering as the primary signal recorded in this technique
questions.feedback: Diffusion MRI/DTI uses water diffusion to investigate the organization of white-matter pathways.

questions.question: What does BOLD stand for?
options: Blood-Optical Light Detection
Brain-Output Localization Difference
Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent
Brain-Oxygen-Level Distribution
questions.feedback: BOLD stands for Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent.

questions.question: What typically happens to deoxyhemoglobin during a positive BOLD response in the deck?
options: It decreases as increased blood flow dilutes and washes it out
It remains constant while only volume changes
It rises because cerebral blood flow falls
It is directly converted into oxyhemoglobin by neurons during the relevant experimental condition
questions.feedback: The deck describes a decrease in deoxyhemoglobin during a typical positive BOLD response.

questions.question: Why is BOLD considered an indirect measure of neural activity?
options: It reflects a vascular response associated with neural activity rather than electrical activity itself
It records magnetic fields generated directly by postsynaptic currents as the principal measurement used here
It infers brain activity only from behavior when the participant is tested in this paradigm
It detects single-neuron action potentials using scalp electrodes during normal developmental testing when the participant is tested in this paradigm
questions.feedback: BOLD reflects hemodynamic changes coupled to neural activity rather than neuronal electrical activity itself.

questions.question: Why does fMRI have poorer temporal resolution than EEG or MEG?
options: MRI requires verbal responses from participants as the principal measurement used here
BOLD measures only spontaneous resting activity during normal developmental testing
The hemodynamic response develops over several seconds
Magnetic resonance cannot detect oxygenation changes as the primary signal recorded in this technique
questions.feedback: The neural event is fast, but the hemodynamic response unfolds over several seconds.

questions.question: What does fNIRS use to estimate cortical hemodynamic changes?
options: Scalp electrical potentials
Near-infrared light
Strong magnetic pulses
Radioactive tracers
questions.feedback: fNIRS uses near-infrared light delivered through the scalp.

questions.question: Which hemoglobin measures are described for fNIRS?
options: Only total hemoglobin and arterial oxygen pressure
Only oxyhemoglobin and cerebral blood flow
Oxyhemoglobin, deoxyhemoglobin, and total hemoglobin
Only deoxyhemoglobin and cerebral blood volume
questions.feedback: The deck lists OHb, DHb, and THb as fNIRS-derived hemoglobin measures.

questions.question: What does total hemoglobin (THb) represent in the fNIRS slide?
options: Hemoglobin contained only in arterial blood
The difference between oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin during the relevant experimental condition
The sum of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin
The amount of oxygen consumed directly by neurons
questions.feedback: THb is presented as the sum of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin.

questions.question: What is an important developmental advantage of fNIRS?
options: It records single-neuron spikes from superficial cortex
It has better spatial resolution than structural MRI
It provides complete coverage of deep brain structures
It is portable, silent, and relatively suitable for infant testing
questions.feedback: The deck emphasizes the accessibility of fNIRS for infant and child testing.

questions.question: What is an important limitation of fNIRS?
options: It always requires a large magnet in the method described in the lecture
It cannot measure hemoglobin changes
It is mainly sensitive to superficial cortex
It requires a radioactive tracer as the primary signal recorded in this technique
questions.feedback: A key limitation is that fNIRS is primarily sensitive to superficial cortical tissue.

questions.question: What does PET use to measure physiological processes?
options: Radioactive tracers whose regional distribution can be detected
Scalp electrical potentials
Magnetic fields from postsynaptic currents
Near-infrared light reflected from cortex
questions.feedback: PET uses radioactive tracers to measure processes such as metabolism or receptor binding.

questions.question: What happens during positron-electron annihilation in PET?
options: Two gamma photons are produced and travel in approximately opposite directions
The positron becomes an electrical potential at the scalp
A single infrared photon is emitted through the scalp
The electron produces a magnetic pulse that stimulates cortex
questions.feedback: Positron-electron annihilation produces two gamma photons emitted in approximately opposite directions.

questions.question: What does coincidence detection in PET identify?
options: The position of a TMS coil
The frequency band of an EEG oscillation in this developmental paradigm
A line of response between two detectors
The latency of an ERP component
questions.feedback: Nearly simultaneous detection of the annihilation photons defines a line of response.

questions.question: Why is PET strongly limited in healthy developmental populations?
options: It requires a head-turn response
It provides no spatial information in the method described in the lecture
It cannot measure metabolism
It exposes participants to ionizing radiation
questions.feedback: PET requires radioactive tracers and therefore exposes participants to ionizing radiation.

questions.question: How is TMS classified in the deck?
options: As a perturbation method that transiently modifies cortical activity
As a peripheral physiological recording method as the principal measurement used here
As a structural neuroimaging technique
As an indirect hemodynamic recording method
questions.feedback: TMS is presented as a perturbation method rather than primarily as a recording method.

questions.question: What physical principle allows TMS to influence cortical tissue?
options: A changing magnetic field induces an electric field in the brain
Scalp electrodes inject current into deep white matter
A radioactive tracer releases gamma photons in cortex
Near-infrared light directly depolarizes neurons
questions.feedback: A rapidly changing magnetic field from the coil induces an electric field in cortical tissue.

questions.question: What kind of inference can TMS strengthen compared with purely recording methods?
options: A causal inference about the contribution of a brain region
An inference about visual acuity from looking
An estimate of total hemoglobin concentration
A measure of spontaneous EEG frequency content
questions.feedback: Because TMS perturbs neural activity and tests the resulting behavioral effect, it can support causal inference.

questions.question: What is the main distinction between recording and perturbation methods in the final slide?
options: Recording methods are always invasive and perturbation methods are never invasive as the main index of the process being studied
Recording methods require adults, whereas perturbation methods are only for infants as the primary signal recorded in this technique
Recording methods measure behavior and perturbation methods measure anatomy as the main index of the process being studied
Recording methods reveal associations, whereas perturbation methods can test causal contributions
questions.feedback: The deck contrasts association from recording methods with stronger causal evidence from perturbation methods such as TMS.
